strengths: The paper targets an important gap: evaluating code-generation models in iterative, dependency-aware workflows rather than only stand-alone function synthesis or monolithic single-turn solutions.

The proposed benchmark is sizable, with 5,258 Codeforces-derived problems, and the pipeline concept of extracting function dependency structure, turn order, subproblem statements, and turn-level tests is potentially useful for future code-generation evaluation.

The evaluation compares a broad set of closed- and open-source models and includes both multi-turn and single-turn settings, making the reported performance gap between the two settings an interesting empirical observation.

The paper introduces useful structural analyses such as overall turns, overall depth, pass depth/APD, and dependency-structure complexity, which are better aligned with iterative code reuse than final pass@1 alone.

The discussion of error types, especially incomplete reasoning versus integration/global-context failures, is relevant and helps clarify why multi-turn code generation can fail differently from single-turn generation.
weaknesses: The strongest concern is evaluation validity: top-level tests are described as using public Codeforces sample tests, and subproblem tests are generated only by executing the reference solution on those inputs. Public samples are typically tiny and non-comprehensive, so pass@1 may not measure true Codeforces correctness or robust functional correctness.

The dataset construction relies heavily on LLM-generated solution code and LLM-generated natural-language subproblem descriptions. Although generated full solutions are submitted to Codeforces, there is little evidence that the decomposition, subproblem statements, dependency extraction, and unit tests are semantically faithful or consistently high quality.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the abstract says the code and dataset will be available soon, and the paper lacks enough detail on prompts, decoding parameters, filtering thresholds, execution harnesses, model versions, and evaluation scripts to independently reproduce the benchmark and results.

The claimed mitigation of data leakage by evaluating the most recent 20% of problems is not convincing without problem dates, model release/cutoff analysis, or contamination checks. Codeforces problems and editorials are widely mirrored and likely included in code/model training data.

The benchmark’s realism claim is only partially supported. Codeforces solutions decomposed into artificial helper functions do not necessarily reflect real software development workflows, maintainability, repository-level constraints, or natural user-driven iterative programming.

The paper does not report human validation of dataset quality, decomposition correctness, generated statements, test adequacy, or annotation agreement for the error taxonomy. The manual error analysis also omits sample size and annotator reliability.
The experimental analysis lacks statistical uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite comparing many models with sometimes small performance differences.

Several methodological details are underspecified, including how model outputs are parsed, how previous incorrect turns affect later turns, whether models see reference or generated prior code, how failures are categorized, how timeouts/runtime errors are handled, and how APD should be interpreted when depth values differ across problems.

The writing is understandable but rough in places, with grammatical errors, formatting issues, inconsistent naming, and some overclaims such as 'first benchmark' and 'high quality' that are not fully substantiated by evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important evaluation gap: multi-turn code generation with explicit reuse of previously implemented functions, which is relevant to current LLM coding workflows.

The benchmark idea is potentially useful, and the dependency-tree framing, pass-depth metric, and multi-turn versus single-turn comparison are sensible starting points for analyzing code-reuse failures.
The paper evaluates a reasonably broad set of closed and open models and reports consistent evidence that multi-turn decomposition is harder than single-turn generation on the constructed tasks.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction is not sufficiently validated. Core artifacts are produced by LLMs from Codeforces editorials, including solution code and natural-language subproblem statements, but the paper provides little evidence of manual quality control, error rates, or robustness of the generated dependency decompositions.

The test methodology is weak. Top-level tests appear to rely on public Codeforces samples, and subproblem tests are generated by tracing one reference solution's function calls. This can miss edge cases, overfit to implementation-specific behavior, and fail to establish semantic correctness of independently generated functions.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The abstract says code and dataset will be available soon, and many experimental details are missing or deferred vaguely to an appendix, including exact prompts, decoding parameters, number of samples for pass@k, sampling procedures, and model versions/API settings.

The central claim that CodeFlowBench reflects real-world software development is overstated. Competitive-programming functions decomposed from generated/editorial solutions do not capture repository-level maintenance, APIs, tests, documentation, or realistic multi-file development, yet the paper repeatedly motivates the benchmark as realistic development codeflow.

The comparison to prior benchmarks is mostly qualitative. The paper does not empirically compare against MTPB, CodeEvalPro, LiveCodeBench, or other relevant resources to substantiate claims of higher difficulty, better coverage, or novelty beyond dataset construction.

The error analysis is under-specified. The paper reports manually annotated error proportions for only two models, but does not state the sample size, annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, or examples sufficient to support the quantitative conclusions.

Some metrics and analyses are questionable. Overall-depth and overall-turns are derived from AST structure of a generated solution rather than inherent problem complexity, and the claimed correlation with Codeforces rating is not quantified in the text. APD may reward shallow partial progress without showing whether generated intermediate functions are generally reusable.

Data leakage and benchmark freshness are not convincingly handled. Codeforces problems and editorials are public and likely present in model pretraining data; selecting the most recent 20% reduces but does not eliminate contamination, and the paper does not perform contamination checks.

Writing and presentation quality are below ACL standards. There are many grammatical errors, formatting problems, unclear definitions, and incomplete statements, which makes the methodology harder to audit.
Overall, the paper has a promising benchmark direction, but the current evidence does not establish a sound and reproducible contribution suitable for Findings without substantial revision.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-evaluated setting: iterative, multi-turn code generation with explicit reuse of previously implemented functions. This is a plausible gap between existing single-shot coding benchmarks and real developer workflows.

CodeFlowBench is large in scale, with 5,258 Codeforces-derived problems, structural labels such as overall turns and depth, unit tests for subproblems, and an automated update pipeline intended to reduce staleness and contamination.

The evaluation framework is more informative than a single final pass@k score. The Average Pass Depth metric and analyses by dependency depth/structure help expose where models fail during multi-turn generation.

The empirical study covers a useful range of closed and open models and reports a consistent, practically relevant finding: models perform much worse in the multi-turn reuse setting than in a single-turn setting over the same underlying problems.

The discussion of error categories, especially instruction misinterpretation and insufficient globalization, is helpful and connects the benchmark results to concrete failure modes in multi-turn code generation.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction depends heavily on LLM-generated artifacts: converting editorials to runnable code and generating natural-language subproblem descriptions. The paper does not provide enough human validation or quantitative quality auditing to establish that these subproblems faithfully reflect the original problem semantics or realistic developer decomposition.

The unit-test generation strategy for subfunctions is potentially weak. Capturing input-output pairs from executions of one reference solution may test behavior only on observed traces rather than the full intended function contract, and may reward reproducing idiosyncrasies of the generated decomposition rather than robust modular code.

The claim of realism is somewhat overstated. Competitive-programming solutions decomposed by AST dependencies are not necessarily representative of maintainable real-world software workflows, even if they create challenging dependency structures.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: the abstract says the code and dataset will be available soon, but without released data, prompts, generated solutions, test cases, model settings, and evaluation harness details, the reported results are difficult to verify.

The comparison between multi-turn and single-turn settings may conflate several factors, including context formatting, exposure to intermediate generated code, error propagation, and differences in how much global information the model can coordinate at once. More ablations would be needed to isolate code reuse ability specifically.

The experimental section uses only the most recent 20% of problems but gives limited detail on selection, sample size after filtering, variance, pass@k sampling parameters, and API/model configuration, which limits confidence in fine-grained model comparisons.
The writing and presentation contain many grammatical issues and some unclear or imprecise claims, which do not invalidate the work but make parts of the methodology harder to assess.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-evaluated capability for code LLMs: iterative function implementation with dependency reuse across turns, which is more realistic than isolated HumanEval-style function generation.

The benchmark design is ambitious, combining a large competitive-programming component with a repository-derived component, and the paper evaluates a broad set of closed and open models under both single-turn and multi-turn settings.

The proposed structural analyses, including pass depth/turn and dependency-structure complexity, are useful diagnostics beyond final pass rate and help reveal where models fail in multi-step code generation.
The paper includes nontrivial pipeline details, prompt templates, cost estimates, sampling statistics, and some ablations/human checks intended to validate the LLM-assisted curation process.
weaknesses: The central validity concern is benchmark construction: canonical solutions, subproblem descriptions, and decompositions are produced or rewritten by LLMs, but the quality validation is limited and permissive. The human/LLM evaluation rubric even instructs judges not to be overly strict and to avoid scores below 2, weakening confidence that generated subproblems are natural, complete, and unambiguous.

Subproblem unit tests are derived from observed calls during execution on public tests, which may provide very sparse and implementation-specific coverage. This risks rewarding compatibility with a particular generated solution rather than the intended subproblem semantics, especially for helper functions with hidden corner cases.

The multi-turn versus single-turn comparison is not fully controlled or convincingly tied to real software workflows. The multi-turn protocol appears to provide previous generated functions without execution feedback or repair, while the single-turn protocol exposes all subproblem descriptions at once; performance gaps may reflect prompt format, error propagation, or decomposition artifacts rather than a clean measure of “codeflow” ability.

The repository component is much smaller than the framing suggests: after filtering, only 70 high-quality multi-turn problems remain before augmentation with single-turn problems. This limits the strength of claims about real-world software-engineering breadth.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The paper says code will be hosted, but does not provide an available artifact, exact evaluation harness, complete generated dataset, model versions/settings, or enough implementation detail to independently reproduce the benchmark and reported results.

Some conclusions are overstated. The paper claims to establish an essential tool and to reveal general model limitations, but the evidence is confounded by LLM-generated tasks, possible Codeforces contamination despite recent sampling, weak helper-function tests, and a small repo subset.
The writing and presentation contain many grammatical errors, formatting issues, and unclear definitions, which make parts of the methodology difficult to audit precisely.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored evaluation setting: multi-turn code generation with explicit reuse of previously implemented functions. This is relevant to NLP/code-generation research and more realistic than isolated single-function benchmarks.

The benchmark construction idea is potentially useful: decomposing solutions into dependency-aware subproblems, providing per-function tests, and reporting both final success and partial-progress metrics could support more diagnostic evaluation if validated carefully.

The experimental coverage is broad, with many closed- and open-source models evaluated under both multi-turn and single-turn settings. The reported performance gap is plausible and highlights a real weakness of current coding models.
The paper includes appendices with pipeline details, prompts, dataset statistics, and cost estimates, which is a good start toward transparency.
weaknesses: The central claims are not adequately supported. The paper claims to benchmark realistic codeflow, but CodeFlowBench-Comp is largely produced by LLM-rewriting Codeforces editorials into modular functions. This may evaluate ability to follow an artificial decomposition rather than real iterative software development or natural code reuse.

The benchmark validity is weakened by heavy dependence on LLM-generated artifacts. DeepSeek-R1 generates canonical modular solutions, DeepSeek-V3 generates subproblem descriptions, and model/LLM judges are used for validation. The ablations do not convincingly rule out bias: ROUGE/BERT-style similarity and very permissive rubric-based judging are insufficient evidence that the generated tasks are accurate, natural, or robust.

The test construction is questionable. Subproblem tests are obtained by tracing function calls on public/sample tests, then deduplicating and capping cases. This can give shallow unit tests with poor coverage and can reward overfitting to observed traces rather than correct general implementations. The paper does not quantify test adequacy or mutation/hidden-test strength for subproblems.

The multi-turn versus single-turn comparison is confounded. The single-turn condition receives all subproblem descriptions at once, while the multi-turn condition suffers from sequential error propagation and stopping after failures. The resulting gap is unsurprising and does not cleanly isolate “codeflow” ability, dependency reuse, or long-context coherence.

CodeFlowBench-Repo is much smaller and less convincing than the framing suggests. Only 70 high-quality multi-turn problems survive filtering, then single-turn problems are added for balance. This is a thin basis for claims about real-world repository-level software engineering across domains.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for a benchmark paper. The manuscript does not provide a concrete release location, exact dataset versioning/update protocol, execution harness details sufficient to reproduce all model evaluations, sample sizes for manual error analysis, or enough detail about decoding settings and model versions.

Several analyses are under-specified or weak. Error-type percentages lack sample sizes and annotation reliability; claims about dependency complexity rely on coarse structural proxies; APD/APT/DSC are not clearly justified as measuring the claimed phenomena; and correlations with Codeforces rating may partly reflect solution length/decomposition artifacts rather than genuine dependency complexity.

The paper overclaims novelty and impact. Prior work on interactive coding, repository-level coding, function-call benchmarks, and multi-turn program synthesis is discussed only shallowly, and the claim of being the first comprehensive benchmark for iterative codeflow needs more careful positioning.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. The manuscript contains many grammar errors, typos, awkward phrasing, inconsistent terminology, and figures with spelling mistakes or low readability. These issues make the methodology harder to trust and the contribution harder to assess.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and under-evaluated capability gap in code generation: iterative, multi-turn implementation with reuse of previously generated functions. The task framing is well motivated and clearly connected to practical software-development workflows.

CodeFlowBench is a useful benchmark contribution with two complementary components: a large Codeforces-derived algorithmic set and a GitHub/DomainEval-derived repository set. This breadth makes the benchmark more informative than a purely competitive-programming or purely repository-level benchmark.

The evaluation is extensive, covering 19 closed- and open-source models under both multi-turn and single-turn settings. The consistent performance degradation in multi-turn settings is a credible and important empirical finding.

The proposed diagnostics, especially pass depth / average pass depth and turn-wise analysis, provide more informative signals than final pass@k alone and help characterize where models fail in dependency-heavy workflows.

The paper includes substantial implementation detail in the appendix, including scraping, decomposition, test generation, sampling, prompt templates, cost estimates, and error analyses. This improves interpretability of the benchmark construction pipeline.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction relies heavily on LLM-generated solution restructuring and LLM-generated subproblem descriptions. Although the paper includes ablations, the validation is not fully convincing: semantic similarity between generated descriptions does not establish task correctness, and the human/LLM evaluation protocol is lenient enough to overestimate quality.

The generated unit tests for subproblems are derived from observed function calls on public/top-level test executions. This may miss important behaviors, overfit to narrow traces, and under-test helper functions, weakening the claim that subproblem pass rates robustly measure correctness.

The CodeFlowBench-Repo component is relatively small after filtering, with only 70 high-quality multi-turn problems plus added single-turn tasks. This limits the strength of claims about real-world repository-level generality, despite the paper’s broad framing.

Reproducibility is promising but not yet fully established in the manuscript. The paper says the code will be hosted and describes Docker use, but it does not provide a clear released artifact, versioned data snapshot, execution scripts, or enough detail to independently reproduce all model evaluations.

The comparison between multi-turn and single-turn settings may conflate task format with prompt/context differences. Single-turn generation receives all subproblem descriptions at once, while multi-turn generation depends on previous outputs and stopping after failures; the paper could better isolate which factors drive the observed degradation.

Some claims are overstated, especially “first benchmark” and “real-world workflow” claims. The task is closer to bottom-up function construction from curated dependency trees than to full iterative software engineering, which also involves debugging, changing requirements, file-level context, and interaction with tests/tools.

The writing is understandable but contains many grammatical issues and occasional imprecision in terminology, metric definitions, and dataset descriptions. These do not undermine the contribution, but they reduce clarity and polish for a main-conference paper.
